title: Fave e Cicoria
subtitle: puglian broad bean puree with bitter greens
excerpt: Fave e cicoria is a Puglian dish of dried broad beans cooked down to a smooth, creamy purée and served alongside sautéed bitter greens dressed with garlic, chilli and olive oil. The contrast between the soft, nutty purée and the sharp greens is the point of the dish. Serves 4.
sourceNotes: Fave e cicoria is one of the oldest and most emblematic dishes of Puglia, eaten by farmers and peasants for centuries. Dried broad beans were a staple crop in the region, and the pairing with wild bitter greens such as cicoria selvatica reflects the cucina povera tradition of using what grew freely. The dish is now considered a symbol of Puglian food identity.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Soak dried broad beans overnight before cooking.

glossaryTerms.definition: Italian for chicory or wild bitter greens, used in southern Italian cooking as a side vegetable or in paired dishes like fave e cicoria.
A smooth, thick paste made by cooking and then processing or mashing ingredients until fully smooth.

content.text: is a two-part dish from Puglia: dried broad beans cooked low and slow until they form a dense, olive-oil-enriched
, paired with bitter greens sautéed with garlic and dried chilli. The broad beans need to be the dried, skinless kind, which cook to a creamy texture without needing to be blended. Serves 4.
Soak the dried broad beans overnight. If you use split dried fava beans they will cook faster, in around 45 minutes. The greens are cooked separately and served alongside, not stirred in.

Drain the soaked broad beans. Put them in a large saucepan and cover with cold water by about 5cm. Bring to a boil, skim any foam, then reduce to a gentle simmer. Cook for 60 to 90 minutes until completely soft and beginning to break down.

Drain off most of the cooking water, leaving a little in the pan. Season to taste, then mash or stir vigorously over low heat until you have a smooth, thick purée. Beat in 4 tablespoons of olive oil. The texture should be thick enough to hold a shape on the plate. Add a splash of the cooking water if needed to loosen.
While the beans cook, bring a separate pan of water to the boil. Blanch the radicchio for 3 to 4 minutes until wilted and tender. Drain well and squeeze out any excess water.
Heat the remaining 2 tablespoons of olive oil in a frying pan. Add the garlic and chilli flakes and fry for 1 minute. Add the drained greens and toss to coat. Season to taste.
Spoon the warm purée onto plates and place the greens alongside. Finish with a drizzle of olive oil.

attrs.symptom: Purée is lumpy rather than smooth
attrs.cause: The beans were not cooked long enough to break down fully
attrs.fix: Keep cooking until the beans are completely soft and beginning to fall apart on their own. A potato masher or vigorous stirring then finishes the job

attrs.symptom: Purée is too thin and watery
attrs.cause: Too much cooking water was left in the pan
attrs.fix: Drain off almost all the water before mashing, adding back just a few tablespoons if the purée becomes too stiff

attrs.symptom: Greens are very bitter and hard to eat
attrs.cause: They were not blanched long enough before sautéing
attrs.fix: The blanching step is there to take the edge off the bitterness. Make sure they are properly wilted and tender before draining

content.text: This dish comes from Puglia, the heel of the Italian boot, where it has been eaten for generations as a cheap and filling staple. It is now found in Pugliese restaurants as a matter of regional pride. The broad beans and greens together make a complete, nourishing plate without any meat or dairy. It is one of the great vegetarian dishes of the Italian south.
